title: How many ways does India measure inflation?
tension: The public hears 'inflation' as a single number, but India publishes a whole zoo of them: headline, core, super-core, food, wholesale, trimmed-mean, the GDP deflator. They can tell opposite stories at the same moment, one screaming, another calm, and which one gets quoted can flip a 'cost-of-living crisis' into 'inflation under control'. Knowing the menu, and what each measure is built to see and built to ignore, is the difference between being informed and being spun.
teachingGoal: Lay out the full menu of India's inflation measures in one place and decode each: what it includes and excludes, who publishes and uses it, and when it is the right number to watch. The reader should be able to hear any inflation figure on the news, know which measure it is, and judge whether it is the one that matters for their question.
sectionArc: Wait, there is more than one inflation number? (the headline is just one of many; why a single index cannot answer every question)
Headline CPI: the one that is law (all-items retail inflation; the RBI's 4% target; now on the new 2024 base, with food's weight down to 36.75%)
CFPI: just the food (the Consumer Food Price Index; food-only; why it is watched, especially for the poor)
Core inflation: stripping out the noise (CPI excluding food and fuel; the persistent, demand-driven trend the RBI steers by)
Super-core: going one level deeper (excluding food, fuel, gold and housing; the cleanest read on underlying demand)
WPI: the wholesale view (producer prices of goods only, no services; its components; why it leads and misleads)
The clever statistical ones: trimmed mean and weighted median (limited-influence measures that drop whatever is spiking this month, not a fixed list; the RBI's cross-checks on core)
And the broadest of all: the GDP deflator (the price of everything an economy produces, not just a consumer basket; how it links to the GDP track)

So which number should you actually watch? (a practical guide: headline for your cost of living, core and super-core for the RBI's read, CFPI if food is most of your budget, WPI for the pipeline, the deflator for the whole economy)
mustTeach: headline CPI is the all-items retail measure and the RBI's legal target (4%, 2-6% band)
core inflation excludes food and fuel; super-core also excludes gold and housing
WPI measures wholesale/producer prices of goods and contains no services
trimmed-mean and weighted-median are 'limited-influence' measures that drop the most extreme movers each month rather than a fixed list
the GDP deflator is the broadest price measure, covering all output, and links to the GDP track
different measures answer different questions; which one to watch depends on the question
featureNumbers: CPI inflation — Consumer Food Price (Combined), latest

contextCards.fact: The Consumer Food Price Index (CFPI) measures retail food inflation on its own. It is built from ten of the twelve sub-groups of the CPI's food and beverages group (leaving out non-alcoholic beverages and prepared meals/snacks), and is watched closely because food is the most volatile and politically charged part of the basket.

Core inflation excludes the volatile food and fuel components to show the persistent, demand-driven trend. Super-core inflation goes further, stripping out food, fuel, gold and housing, to isolate the cleanest signal of underlying demand pressure. Both are analytical measures the RBI and economists watch; neither is the official headline.
contextCards.source: RBI / standard central-banking practice on core and super-core inflation (verified)

contextCards.fact: Beyond simple exclusion, the RBI also publishes 'limited-influence' measures of underlying inflation. The trimmed mean drops the items with the most extreme price moves each month (the biggest risers and fallers) and averages the rest. The weighted median takes the inflation rate of the single item sitting at the midpoint of all the price changes. Unlike core, which always excludes the same items, these let the excluded set change month to month depending on whatever is spiking.
contextCards.source: RBI measures of core/underlying inflation; trimmed-mean and weighted-median methodology (verified)

contextCards.fact: The broadest inflation measure of all is the GDP deflator: the price change across everything an economy produces, not just a consumer basket, derived by comparing nominal and real GDP. It covers investment goods, government services and exports too, and is used to convert nominal GDP into real GDP.
contextCards.source: Standard national-accounts methodology (GDP deflator); see the GDP track

contextCards.fact: The Wholesale Price Index is dominated by manufactured products (about 64% of its basket), with primary articles (about 23%) and fuel and power (about 13%). It contains no services at all, which is one reason India switched its monetary-policy anchor from WPI to CPI.
contextCards.source: Office of the Economic Adviser, WPI 2011-12 weights (verified)

contextCards.fact: On 12 February 2026 India launched a new Consumer Price Index series with base year 2024 (replacing 2012), built on the Household Consumption Expenditure Survey of 2023-24. Food and beverages fell from 45.86% to 36.75% of the basket as Indians spend more on services; the basket grew from 299 to 358 items, adding e-commerce, telecom data and OTT subscriptions, and adopted the international COICOP classification. Headline inflation on the new base was 2.75% in January 2026.
contextCards.source: MoSPI / NSO, first CPI release on base 2024=100, 12 February 2026; HCES 2023-24
